sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This counts every row in the CRM opportunities table, i.e. all opportunities on record regardless of stage (won, lost, or still open). If you meant only currently open deals, we'd filter to is_closed = false instead.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT account) AS account_count FROM crm_accounts
explanation: This counts the distinct client accounts listed in the CRM accounts table. Each row is one company account with its sector, size, and location details.

sql: SELECT series, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM crm_products GROUP BY series ORDER BY product_count DESC
explanation: This counts the products listed in the CRM product catalogue within each series, sorted from largest to smallest series.

sql: SELECT SUM(close_value) AS total_won_value, COUNT(*) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won
explanation: This sums the close value of every CRM opportunity flagged as won, and also reports how many such deals there are. Only won deals are included; open and lost deals are excluded.

sql: SELECT deal_stage, COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY deal_stage ORDER BY opportunity_count DESC
explanation: This counts every sales opportunity grouped by its deal stage, sorted from most to fewest. No filters applied, so all opportunities are included.

sql: SELECT AVG(close_value) AS avg_won_deal_value, COUNT(*) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won
explanation: This averages the close value across all CRM opportunities flagged as won. Deals that were lost or still open are excluded, so the figure reflects only successfully closed business.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS closed_deals, SUM(CASE WHEN is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won_deals, SUM(CASE WHEN is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_closed
explanation: This counts all closed CRM opportunities and the share of them that were won. Deals still open are excluded, so the rate reflects only decided outcomes.

sql: SELECT sales_agent, SUM(close_value) AS won_value, COUNT(*) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won AND close_value IS NOT NULL GROUP BY sales_agent ORDER BY won_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This sums the closed value of won opportunities per sales agent and returns the five agents with the highest totals. Only deals marked as won are counted, so open or lost opportunities are excluded.

sql: SELECT a.sector, COUNT(*) AS closed_deals, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won_deals, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS win_rate_pct FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON a.account = o.account WHERE o.is_closed GROUP BY a.sector ORDER BY win_rate_pct DESC
explanation: For each account sector, this counts closed opportunities and the share of them that were won. Only closed deals are included, so open/in-progress opportunities do not dilute the rate; deals for accounts not present in the accounts table are excluded.

sql: SELECT median(cycle_days) AS median_cycle_days FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won AND cycle_days IS NOT NULL
explanation: This finds the middle value of the sales cycle length (days from engagement to close) across all CRM opportunities that were won. Deals with no recorded cycle length are excluded.

sql: SELECT manager, COUNT(DISTINCT sales_agent) AS agents FROM crm_sales_teams GROUP BY manager ORDER BY agents DESC
explanation: Counts the distinct sales agents listed under each manager in the sales teams table, sorted from largest team to smallest.

sql: SELECT t.regional_office, COUNT(*) AS won_deals, SUM(o.close_value) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_sales_teams t ON o.sales_agent = t.sales_agent WHERE o.is_won GROUP BY t.regional_office ORDER BY booked_value DESC
explanation: This sums the close value of won opportunities, grouped by the regional office of the sales agent who owned each deal. Only won (booked) deals are counted; open and lost deals are excluded.

sql: SELECT product, series, list_price FROM crm_products WHERE list_price > 3000 ORDER BY list_price DESC
explanation: This lists every product in the CRM product catalogue whose list price exceeds 3000, along with its series, sorted from most to least expensive.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunities_without_account FROM crm_opportunities WHERE account IS NULL OR TRIM(account) = ''
explanation: Counts rows in the CRM opportunities table where the account field is missing (null or blank). This is a simple data-completeness count, not filtered by deal stage or date.

sql: SELECT p.series, MEDIAN(o.close_value) AS median_won_value, COUNT(*) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_products p ON p.product = o.product WHERE o.is_won = TRUE GROUP BY p.series ORDER BY median_won_value DESC
explanation: This takes only won opportunities in the CRM pipeline, joins them to the product catalogue to get each product's series, and reports the median closing value plus the number of won deals per series. Lost and still-open deals are excluded.

sql: SELECT date_trunc('month', close_date) AS close_month, COUNT(*) AS deals_closed FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_closed = TRUE AND close_date >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND close_date < DATE '2018-01-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Counts CRM opportunities that reached a closed state, grouped by the month of their close date, restricted to 2017. Both won and lost deals are included since "closed" covers either outcome.

sql: SELECT account, employees, office_location, revenue_musd, year_established FROM crm_accounts WHERE lower(sector) = 'technology' AND employees > 5000 ORDER BY employees DESC
explanation: This lists CRM accounts whose sector is recorded as "technology" and whose employee count exceeds 5,000, sorted from largest to smallest headcount. Only accounts with a sector value of exactly "technology" are included.

sql: SELECT t.manager, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE o.is_closed = 1) AS closed_opportunities, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE o.is_won = 1) AS won_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_sales_teams t ON o.sales_agent = t.sales_agent GROUP BY t.manager ORDER BY closed_opportunities DESC
explanation: For each sales manager, this counts the opportunities handled by their agents that reached a closed state, and how many of those were won. Opportunities are attributed to a manager through the sales agent assignment in the sales teams table.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_opportunities, SUM(CASE WHEN is_closed = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS open_opportunities, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN is_closed = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS pct_open FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This counts all sales opportunities and the subset not yet closed (is_closed = 0), then expresses the open ones as a percentage of the total. No date or other filters applied, so it covers the full opportunity table.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS subsidiary_accounts FROM crm_accounts WHERE parent_account IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(parent_account) <> ''
explanation: This counts accounts in the CRM account list that have a parent company recorded, i.e. subsidiaries. Accounts with a blank or missing parent are treated as independent.

sql: SELECT a.sector, AVG(o.close_value) AS avg_won_deal_value, COUNT(*) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON a.account = o.account WHERE o.is_won AND o.close_value IS NOT NULL GROUP BY a.sector ORDER BY avg_won_deal_value DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: This finds the average close value of won opportunities grouped by the account's sector, and returns the top sector. Only won deals with a recorded close value are counted; opportunities not linked to a known account are excluded.

sql: SELECT account, SUM(close_value) AS booked_value, COUNT(*) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won AND account IS NOT NULL GROUP BY account ORDER BY booked_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This sums the closed value of won opportunities for each account and returns the top five. Only deals marked as won are counted, so open or lost pipeline is excluded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT mql_id) AS marketing_qualified_leads FROM funnel_leads
explanation: This counts the distinct marketing-qualified lead IDs recorded in the marketing funnel leads table, which is the full set of MQLs that entered the funnel.

sql: SELECT CASE WHEN is_won THEN 'Won' ELSE 'Lost' END AS outcome, COUNT(*) AS deals, MEDIAN(cycle_days) AS median_cycle_days FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_closed AND cycle_days IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: This compares the median sales cycle length (days from engagement to close) for won versus lost deals in the CRM opportunity pipeline. Only closed deals with a recorded cycle length are included, since open deals have no final cycle duration.

sql: SELECT SUM(p.list_price) AS open_pipeline_list_price_value, COUNT(*) AS open_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_products p ON o.product = p.product WHERE o.is_closed = 0
explanation: This sums the catalogue list price of the product attached to each opportunity that is still open (not closed), giving a list-price valuation of the current pipeline rather than the agents' quoted deal values. Opportunities whose product does not match the product catalogue are excluded by the join.

sql: SELECT origin AS acquisition_channel, COUNT(*) AS leads FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY origin ORDER BY leads DESC
explanation: Counts marketing qualified leads in the funnel_leads table grouped by their origin (acquisition channel), highest volume first. Each row is one lead; channels recorded as unknown or missing appear as their own group.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_leads, COUNT(won_date) AS signed_clients, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(won_date) / COUNT(*), 2) AS conversion_pct FROM funnel_leads LEFT JOIN funnel_deals USING (mql_id)
explanation: This counts all marketing-qualified leads and how many of them have a closed-won date in the deals table, plus the conversion rate. A lead is treated as a signed client when it appears in funnel_deals with a won date.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS qualified_leads, COUNT(won_date) AS converted_leads, ROUND(COUNT(won_date) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS conversion_rate_pct FROM funnel_leads
explanation: This counts all marketing-qualified leads and the subset that reached a signed/won date (recorded in the closed-deals table), then expresses conversions as a percentage. Leads without a won date are treated as not converted; note that very recent leads may still be in progress.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS signed_clients, SUM(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ever_generated_revenue, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS pct_ever_sold FROM deal_outcomes WHERE won_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: Among closed-won leads (those with a won date) in deal_outcomes, this counts how many ever recorded a sale and expresses that as a percentage. Leads that were never signed are excluded.

sql: SELECT median(days_to_close) AS median_days_to_close, count(*) AS closed_deals FROM funnel_deals WHERE won_date IS NOT NULL AND days_to_close IS NOT NULL
explanation: This gives the median elapsed days between a lead's first contact and the date the deal was won (signed), using only closed-won deals in the funnel table. Deals never won are excluded, since they have no signature date.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders FROM orders
explanation: This counts every row in the orders table, giving the total number of orders on record regardless of status (including cancelled or unavailable ones).

sql: SELECT business_segment, COUNT(DISTINCT mql_id) AS signed_clients FROM funnel_deals GROUP BY business_segment ORDER BY signed_clients DESC LIMIT 10
explanation: Counts closed-won leads (signed clients) recorded in the deals table, grouped by their business segment, and shows the ten largest segments. Each row in funnel_deals is a lead that became a signed client, identified by its unique mql_id.

sql: SELECT origin AS channel, COUNT(*) AS signed_clients, SUM(revenue_90d) AS revenue_first_90d, AVG(revenue_90d) AS avg_revenue_per_client FROM deal_outcomes WHERE ever_sold AND window_complete GROUP BY origin ORDER BY revenue_first_90d DESC
explanation: This sums the first-90-day revenue of leads that were won and went on to sell, grouped by the marketing channel (origin) that produced the lead. Only clients whose full 90-day window has elapsed are included, so the comparison is like-for-like; recently signed clients are excluded.

sql: SELECT SUM(oi.price) AS total_item_revenue FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id WHERE o.order_status <> 'canceled'
explanation: This sums the item price of every line item belonging to orders whose status is not "canceled". Freight charges are excluded, so this is product revenue only.

sql: SELECT AVG(review_score) AS avg_review_score FROM order_reviews
explanation: This takes the simple average of all customer review scores (1-5 scale) across every review in the order_reviews table, with no filters applied.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_with_multiple_item_lines FROM (SELECT order_id FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) t
explanation: This counts orders in the order_items table that have two or more item lines. Each row in order_items is one item line, so orders grouped with a count above one are included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_unique_id) AS unique_customers FROM customers
explanation: Counts distinct customer_unique_id values in the customers table, which identifies real individual customers (the customer_id column instead identifies one customer per order).

sql: SELECT c.customer_state, COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY c.customer_state ORDER BY delivered_orders DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: Counts orders with status 'delivered', grouped by the customer's state, and returns the top five states. Orders are attributed to the state of the buying customer, not the seller.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS signed_clients_with_complete_window FROM deal_outcomes WHERE ever_sold AND window_complete
explanation: Counts leads in deal_outcomes that were signed (ever_sold) and whose 90-day post-signing observation window is fully elapsed (window_complete). Rows without a complete window are excluded, so this is a subset of all signed clients.

sql: SELECT AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', order_purchase_timestamp, order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_days_to_delivery, COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders FROM orders WHERE order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL AND order_purchase_timestamp IS NOT NULL
explanation: This averages the number of days from when a customer placed an order to when it was delivered to them. Only orders with both a purchase and an actual delivery timestamp are included, so undelivered or cancelled orders are excluded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders, SUM(CASE WHEN order_delivered_customer_date <= order_estimated_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS on_time_orders, 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN order_delivered_customer_date <= order_estimated_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS on_time_pct FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'delivered' AND order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL AND order_estimated_delivery_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: Among orders with status "delivered" that have both an actual delivery date and an estimated delivery date, this counts how many arrived on or before the estimate and expresses that as a percentage. Orders missing either date are excluded.

sql: SELECT l.origin AS channel, COUNT(*) AS leads, COUNT(d.mql_id) AS signed_clients, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(d.mql_id) / COUNT(*), 2) AS conversion_rate_pct FROM funnel_leads l LEFT JOIN funnel_deals d ON l.mql_id = d.mql_id GROUP BY l.origin ORDER BY conversion_rate_pct DESC
explanation: For each marketing origin (channel), this counts all marketing-qualified leads and how many of them appear in the closed-deal table, then expresses the latter as a percentage of leads. Leads with no matching deal are counted as not converted.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS leads_without_origin FROM funnel_leads WHERE origin IS NULL OR lower(trim(origin)) IN ('', 'other', 'unknown')
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads in the lead table whose acquisition channel ("origin") is missing — either null, blank, or explicitly recorded as unknown/other. If you want strictly missing values only, the 'other'/'unknown' labels should be excluded from the filter.

sql:
SELECT s.seller_state, SUM(sp.revenue_brl) AS total_revenue_brl
FROM seller_performance sp
JOIN sellers s ON s.seller_id = sp.seller_id
GROUP BY s.seller_state
ORDER BY total_revenue_brl DESC
LIMIT 5
explanation: This sums each seller's lifetime revenue (in BRL, from the seller performance table) and groups it by the seller's home state, showing the five states with the highest totals. Revenue is attributed to the seller's registered state, not the buyer's location.

sql:
SELECT business_segment,
       COUNT(*) AS clients,
       SUM(CASE WHEN revenue_lifetime > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS clients_with_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN revenue_lifetime > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS revenue_attachment_rate_pct
FROM deal_outcomes
WHERE business_segment IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY business_segment
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20
ORDER BY revenue_attachment_rate_pct DESC
explanation: This lists business segments in the deal outcomes table and shows what share of their clients ever generated lifetime revenue ("revenue attachment rate"), keeping only segments with at least 20 clients. Segments are ranked from highest to lowest attachment rate.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS cancelled_orders FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'canceled'
explanation: This counts rows in the orders table whose status is recorded as "canceled". It covers the marketplace order data only, not CRM deals.

sql: SELECT o.order_status, AVG(r.review_score) AS avg_review_score, COUNT(*) AS reviews FROM orders o JOIN order_reviews r ON r.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.order_status ORDER BY avg_review_score DESC
explanation: This joins reviews to their orders and averages the 1-5 review score within each order status, along with how many reviews contribute to each average. Orders without reviews are excluded.

sql: SELECT lead_type, COUNT(*) AS signed_clients FROM funnel_deals GROUP BY lead_type ORDER BY signed_clients DESC
explanation: Every row in funnel_deals is a lead that was signed (closed as a client), so counting rows by lead_type gives the number of signed clients per lead type. Lead types with no recorded value appear as a null group.

sql: SELECT median(revenue_90d) AS median_revenue_90d, COUNT(*) AS sellers_counted FROM deal_outcomes WHERE ever_sold AND revenue_90d > 0
explanation: This takes the median of the 90-day revenue figure in deal_outcomes, restricted to closed-won leads that actually generated revenue in that window (revenue_90d greater than zero). Leads with no sales or zero revenue are excluded, so the median reflects only revenue-producing clients.

sql: SELECT product_category_name_english, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products WHERE product_category_name_english IS NOT NULL GROUP BY product_category_name_english ORDER BY product_count DESC LIMIT 10
explanation: This counts catalog products grouped by their English category name and lists the ten categories with the most products. Products with a missing English category name are excluded.

sql: SELECT date_trunc('month', first_contact_date) AS contact_month, COUNT(DISTINCT mql_id) AS leads FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: This counts distinct marketing-qualified leads by the month of their first contact, using the lead intake table. Months with no leads simply do not appear.

sql: SELECT s.seller_id, s.seller_city, s.seller_state, sp.revenue_brl, sp.orders, sp.avg_review_score FROM seller_performance sp LEFT JOIN sellers s ON s.seller_id = sp.seller_id ORDER BY sp.revenue_brl DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This lists the five sellers with the largest total revenue (in BRL) recorded in the seller performance table, along with their order counts and average customer review score. Sellers with no reviews would show a blank average score.

sql: SELECT AVG(order_total) AS avg_order_value FROM (SELECT order_id, SUM(price) AS order_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) t
explanation: This first totals the item prices for each order, then averages those order totals, so every order counts once regardless of how many items it contains. Freight/shipping charges are excluded — only product prices are included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS signed_clients_no_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE ever_sold AND window_complete AND COALESCE(revenue_90d, 0) = 0
explanation: Counts closed/won (signed) leads in deal_outcomes whose 90-day revenue is zero. Only leads with a complete 90-day observation window are included, so recently signed clients that haven't had a full 90 days yet are excluded.

sql: SELECT landing_page_id, COUNT(DISTINCT mql_id) AS leads FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY landing_page_id ORDER BY leads DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This counts the distinct marketing qualified leads attributed to each landing page in the lead funnel table, and returns the five landing pages with the highest lead counts.

sql: SELECT business_type, COUNT(*) AS won_deals, AVG(days_to_close) AS avg_days_to_close FROM funnel_deals WHERE days_to_close IS NOT NULL GROUP BY business_type ORDER BY avg_days_to_close
explanation: This shows, for each business type of closed/won funnel deals, the average number of days between first contact and the won date. Only deals with a recorded days-to-close value are included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders_with_score_1 FROM order_reviews WHERE review_score = 1
explanation: Counts the distinct orders that received a review with the lowest score of 1. Orders with multiple reviews are counted once; orders with no review are excluded.

sql: SELECT lead_type, COUNT(*) AS clients, AVG(revenue_90d) AS avg_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete AND ever_sold GROUP BY lead_type ORDER BY avg_revenue_90d DESC
explanation: This averages the first-90-day revenue for won clients whose 90-day observation window has fully elapsed (window_complete), grouped by lead type. Restricting to completed windows avoids understating revenue for recently won deals; only clients that actually sold are included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT seller_id) AS distinct_sellers FROM order_items
explanation: This counts the unique seller identifiers appearing across all order item lines, showing how many distinct sellers have sold at least one item.

sql: SELECT business_segment, SUM(revenue_90d) AS total_revenue_90d, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM deal_outcomes WHERE business_segment IS NOT NULL GROUP BY business_segment ORDER BY total_revenue_90d DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This sums the 90-day revenue recorded for each closed-deal business segment and returns the five highest totals. Deals with no business segment recorded are excluded.

sql: SELECT AVG(freight_value) AS avg_freight_per_item_line, COUNT(*) AS item_lines FROM order_items
explanation: This averages the freight_value across every order item line in the order_items table, giving the typical shipping cost charged per individual item line. It includes all item lines regardless of order status.

There is no sign-in, login, or account-registration event data in these tables. Customers appear only via orders (with purchase timestamps), and CRM accounts have only a year established — neither records a client "signing in" or signing up on a given date.

sql: SELECT c.customer_state, COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders, AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', o.order_purchase_timestamp, o.order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_delivery_days FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_status = 'delivered' AND o.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c.customer_state HAVING COUNT(*) >= 500 AND AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', o.order_purchase_timestamp, o.order_delivered_customer_date)) > 20 ORDER BY avg_delivery_days DESC
explanation: For each customer state, this counts delivered orders and computes the average number of days from purchase to customer delivery. Only states with at least 500 delivered orders and an average above 20 days are shown, sorted slowest first.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS avg_item_lines_per_order FROM order_items
explanation: This counts all item lines in the order_items table and divides by the number of distinct orders, giving the average number of item lines per order. Orders with no items recorded are not included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS signed_clients, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE origin = 'paid_search') AS paid_search_clients, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE origin = 'paid_search') / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2) AS pct_paid_search FROM funnel_deals
explanation: Signed clients are the closed/won deals recorded in funnel_deals (each row is a lead that became a client). The query counts how many of those originated from the "paid_search" acquisition channel and expresses it as a percentage of all signed clients. Leads with unknown/missing origin are counted in the denominator.

sql: SELECT seller_id, reviews FROM seller_performance ORDER BY reviews DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5
explanation: This lists the five sellers with the highest count of reviews recorded in the seller performance table, sorted from most to fewest.

sql: SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY order_status ORDER BY order_count DESC
explanation: This counts every order in the orders table, grouped by its status (delivered, shipped, canceled, etc.), sorted from most to least common. No filters are applied, so all orders are included.

sql: SELECT origin, COUNT(*) AS sellers_observed, SUM(CASE WHEN revenue_lifetime > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS sellers_with_revenue, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN revenue_lifetime > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS revenue_attachment_rate_pct FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY origin ORDER BY revenue_attachment_rate_pct DESC
explanation: For each acquisition channel (origin), this shows the share of closed/observed clients that went on to generate any lifetime revenue. Only clients whose observation window is complete are included, so recently acquired clients with insufficient tracking time are excluded.

sql: SELECT SUM(revenue_90d) AS total_revenue_90d, COUNT(*) AS leads FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete
explanation: This sums the 90-day revenue recorded in deal_outcomes, restricted to leads whose 90-day observation window is complete, so partially observed leads don't understate the total. It also reports how many such leads are included.

sql:
SELECT behaviour_primary, COUNT(*) AS signed_clients
FROM funnel_deals
WHERE behaviour_primary IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY behaviour_primary
ORDER BY signed_clients DESC
explanation: This counts closed/won deals (signed clients) in the funnel_deals table by their primary lead behaviour profile, ranked from most to least common. The top row is the most common profile; rows with no recorded profile are excluded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS sellers_below_3 FROM seller_performance WHERE avg_review_score < 3
explanation: This counts sellers in the seller performance table whose average review score is below 3. Sellers with no reviews (null average score) are excluded, since they have no score to compare.

sql: SELECT MAX(days_to_close) AS longest_days_to_close FROM funnel_deals WHERE won_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: This returns the maximum number of days between first contact and the signing date among closed (won) deals in the marketing funnel table. Only deals with a recorded won date are counted.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This counts every sales opportunity recorded in the CRM pipeline, whether still open (Prospecting or Engaging) or already closed as Won or Lost. No filters applied, so it is the full pipeline total.

sql: SELECT series AS product_series, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM crm_products GROUP BY series ORDER BY product_count DESC
explanation: This counts the products listed in the CRM product catalogue within each product family (GTX, MG, GTK). No filters applied — it covers the whole catalogue.

sql: SELECT crm_opportunities.deal_stage AS deal_stage, COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY crm_opportunities.deal_stage ORDER BY opportunity_count DESC
explanation: This counts every sales opportunity in the CRM pipeline, grouped by its stage (Prospecting, Engaging, Won, Lost). No filters applied, so both open and closed opportunities are included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS account_count FROM crm_accounts
explanation: This counts the client companies listed in the sales pipeline's account list — one row per account. It covers the CRM (synthetic hardware vendor) domain only, and includes all accounts whether or not any opportunity was opened against them.

sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN crm_opportunities.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This totals the closing value of every opportunity marked as won in the 2017 sales pipeline. Lost and still-open deals contribute nothing to the total. Note this is the synthetic teaching dataset, so it describes pipeline shape rather than a real market.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN crm_opportunities.close_value END) AS avg_won_value FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This gives the average close value across all won opportunities in the 2017 sales pipeline. Lost deals (recorded as zero) and open deals (no value yet) are excluded so they don't pull the average down. Note this is a synthetic teaching dataset, so the figure describes pipeline shape only.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate, COUNT(*) AS closed_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities WHERE crm_opportunities.is_closed
explanation: This gives the share of closed sales opportunities that were won, in the synthetic CRM pipeline. Only closed deals are counted — open (Prospecting/Engaging) deals are excluded because their outcome isn't known yet, and including them would understate the rate. The count of closed opportunities is shown alongside so the figure can be judged for precision.

sql: SELECT crm_opportunities.sales_agent, SUM(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN crm_opportunities.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY crm_opportunities.sales_agent ORDER BY booked_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This ranks sales agents by the total value of the deals they won in the 2017 pipeline, showing the top five. Lost and still-open opportunities contribute nothing to the total. Note this is the synthetic CRM teaching dataset, so it describes pipeline shape only.

sql: SELECT a.sector, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate, COUNT(*) AS closed_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON o.account = a.account WHERE o.is_closed GROUP BY a.sector ORDER BY win_rate DESC
explanation: This shows, for each industry sector of the client accounts, the share of closed opportunities that were won. Only closed deals are counted — still-open opportunities are excluded because their outcome isn't known yet — and opportunities with no named account are excluded. The closed-deal counts are shown alongside because differences between sectors in this dataset are generally within sampling noise, and this pipeline data is synthetic.

sql: SELECT t.regional_office, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_sales_teams t ON o.sales_agent = t.sales_agent GROUP BY t.regional_office ORDER BY booked_value DESC
explanation: This totals the value of won deals in the 2017 sales pipeline, grouped by the regional office of the agent who owned the deal. Lost and still-open opportunities contribute nothing to the total. Note this is the synthetic teaching dataset, so it describes pipeline shape only.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(crm_opportunities.cycle_days) AS median_cycle_days FROM crm_opportunities WHERE crm_opportunities.cycle_days IS NOT NULL AND crm_opportunities.is_won
explanation: This gives the typical (median) number of days from engaging a prospect to closing, counting only opportunities that were won. Opportunities with no recorded cycle length — notably deals still in Prospecting, which never have an engagement date — are excluded. The median is used because the distribution is skewed, so an average would not describe a real deal.

sql: SELECT product, series, list_price FROM crm_products WHERE list_price > 3000 ORDER BY list_price DESC
explanation: This lists every product in the sales catalogue whose list price is above 3,000, along with its product family, ordered from most to least expensive. It comes from the synthetic sales pipeline catalogue, so it describes the fictitious hardware vendor's product list only.

sql: SELECT manager, COUNT(DISTINCT sales_agent) AS agent_count FROM crm_sales_teams GROUP BY manager ORDER BY agent_count DESC
explanation: This counts the number of distinct sales agents listed under each manager in the CRM sales team roster, sorted from largest team to smallest. No filters are applied, so every agent in the roster is included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities WHERE account IS NULL OR TRIM(account) = ''
explanation: This counts sales pipeline opportunities that name no client account (blank or missing). These rows must be excluded from any account-level analysis; the documented figure is 1,425.

sql: SELECT account, employees, office_location, revenue_musd FROM crm_accounts WHERE lower(sector) = 'technology' AND employees > 5000 ORDER BY employees DESC
explanation: This lists client accounts in the CRM account list whose industry is technology and whose headcount is above 5,000, largest first, with their location and reported revenue. It is a simple listing of accounts, not a measure of pipeline activity.

sql: SELECT strftime(crm_opportunities.close_date, '%Y-%m') AS close_month, COUNT(*) AS closed_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities WHERE crm_opportunities.is_closed AND crm_opportunities.close_date >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND crm_opportunities.close_date < DATE '2018-01-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: This counts closed sales opportunities (won or lost) by the month they closed during 2017, in the synthetic CRM pipeline. Open opportunities (Prospecting or Engaging) are excluded because they have no close date.

sql: SELECT crm_products.series AS product_series, MEDIAN(crm_opportunities.close_value) AS median_won_value, COUNT(*) AS won_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities JOIN crm_products ON crm_opportunities.product = crm_products.product WHERE crm_opportunities.is_won GROUP BY crm_products.series ORDER BY median_won_value DESC
explanation: This shows the typical (median) closing value of won deals, grouped by product family (GTX, MG, GTK), along with how many won deals sit behind each figure. Only deals actually won are included — lost deals (recorded as zero value) and still-open deals are excluded, since including them would distort the typical won-deal value. Note this is the synthetic CRM pipeline dataset, describing pipeline shape only.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_closed THEN 0.0 ELSE 1.0 END) AS open_share, COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This measures the proportion of all sales opportunities in the 2017 pipeline that are not yet closed (i.e. still in Prospecting or Engaging), alongside the total opportunity count. No filters are applied, so every opportunity is included whether or not it names an account.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS subsidiary_accounts FROM crm_accounts WHERE parent_account IS NOT NULL
explanation: This counts client accounts in the sales pipeline dataset that have a parent company recorded, i.e. subsidiaries. Accounts with no parent listed are treated as standalone.

sql: SELECT t.manager, COUNT(*) AS closed_opportunities, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won_opportunities, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_sales_teams t ON o.sales_agent = t.sales_agent WHERE o.is_closed GROUP BY t.manager ORDER BY closed_opportunities DESC
explanation: For each manager, this counts the opportunities their agents brought to a close (won or lost) and how many of those were won, plus the resulting win rate. Only closed opportunities are counted — deals still in Prospecting or Engaging have no outcome yet. Differences in win rate between managers in this teaching dataset are small enough to sit within sampling noise.

sql: SELECT a.sector, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value END) AS avg_won_value, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE o.is_won) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON o.account = a.account GROUP BY a.sector HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE o.is_won) > 0 ORDER BY avg_won_value DESC
explanation: This ranks client sectors by the mean value of deals actually won, with the top row being the highest. Only opportunities that name a client account are included (about 1,425 opportunities have no account and are left out), and lost or still-open deals do not affect the average. Note this is the synthetic sales-pipeline dataset, and sector differences here are small relative to sampling noise.

sql: SELECT deal_stage, MEDIAN(cycle_days) AS median_cycle_days, COUNT(*) AS opportunities FROM crm_opportunities WHERE cycle_days IS NOT NULL AND deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost') GROUP BY deal_stage ORDER BY deal_stage
explanation: This shows the typical (median) number of days from engagement to close, split between won and lost opportunities in the 2017 sales pipeline. Opportunities without a recorded cycle length (all still-open deals, which never engaged or closed) are excluded, since cycle time is undefined for them.

sql: SELECT SUM(crm_products.list_price) AS open_pipeline_list_value, COUNT(*) AS open_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities JOIN crm_products ON crm_opportunities.product = crm_products.product WHERE crm_opportunities.deal_stage IN ('Prospecting', 'Engaging')
explanation: This adds up the catalogue list price of the product attached to each still-open opportunity (those in Prospecting or Engaging), giving the list-price value of the open pipeline, along with how many open opportunities it covers. It uses list prices rather than actual close values, since open deals have no close value recorded yet.

sql: SELECT crm_opportunities.account AS account_name, SUM(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN crm_opportunities.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities WHERE crm_opportunities.account IS NOT NULL GROUP BY crm_opportunities.account ORDER BY booked_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This ranks client accounts by the total value of their won deals; lost and still-open opportunities contribute nothing. Opportunities that name no account are excluded, since they cannot be attributed to a client. Figures come from the synthetic CRM pipeline dataset.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads
explanation: This counts every marketing-qualified lead recorded in the acquisition funnel (June 2017 to November 2018). No filters applied, so it is the full lead population.

sql: SELECT funnel_leads.origin AS channel, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY funnel_leads.origin ORDER BY lead_count DESC
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads by the channel that produced them, highest first. Note that 'unknown' means the source could not be identified, while 'not_recorded' means no source was captured at all — they are kept separate.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS conversion_rate FROM funnel_leads LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes ON funnel_leads.mql_id = deal_outcomes.mql_id
explanation: This measures the share of all marketing-qualified leads that went on to become signed clients. It counts every qualified lead in the denominator, since a lead either signed or did not — nothing here is cut short by when the data ends.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN deal_outcomes.ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete
explanation: This gives the attachment rate: the share of signed clients that went on to bill any revenue. It counts only clients that had a full 90-day observation window — a required filter, since clients signed near the end of the data could not yet show revenue, and including them would understate the rate (45.0% instead of 51.4%).

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) AS signed_clients, COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS leads, COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS conversion_rate FROM funnel_leads LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes ON funnel_leads.mql_id = deal_outcomes.mql_id
explanation: This counts all marketing-qualified leads, how many of them went on to sign as clients, and the resulting conversion share. No time or completeness filter is applied, since whether a lead signs is not affected by when the data ends.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(deal_outcomes.days_to_close) AS median_days_to_close FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This gives the typical (median) number of days between a lead's first marketing contact and the date the client signed, across all signed clients in the acquisition data (June 2017 to November 2018). The median is used rather than the average because a few very long journeys would distort a mean.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count FROM orders
explanation: This counts every distinct order in the marketplace order records, across all statuses (including cancelled ones, since no revenue is being measured here).

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.business_segment, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY deal_outcomes.business_segment ORDER BY deal_count DESC LIMIT 10
explanation: This counts signed clients in each business segment and shows the ten largest segments. All signed deals are included, with no observation-window filter, since this is a simple count rather than a rate.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.origin AS channel, SUM(deal_outcomes.revenue_90d) AS revenue_90d, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete GROUP BY deal_outcomes.origin ORDER BY revenue_90d DESC
explanation: This totals the revenue that newly signed clients billed within their first 90 days, broken out by the acquisition channel that produced the lead. Only deals with a complete 90-day observation window are included — deals signed too close to the end of the data cannot show revenue, so including them would understate channels. Note that 'unknown' means the source could not be identified and 'not_recorded' means it was missing; they are kept separate.

sql: SELECT SUM(order_items.price) AS order_revenue FROM order_items JOIN orders ON order_items.order_id = orders.order_id WHERE orders.order_status <> 'canceled'
explanation: This totals the item prices on all orders that were not cancelled. Freight is excluded because it is a pass-through cost rather than seller revenue, and cancelled orders are left out as required.

sql: SELECT AVG(order_reviews.review_score) AS avg_review_score FROM order_reviews
explanation: This gives the mean customer review score, on the 1-to-5 scale, across all reviews in the marketplace data. No filters are applied, so every recorded review counts once.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_with_multiple_item_lines FROM (SELECT order_items.order_id FROM order_items GROUP BY order_items.order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) t
explanation: This counts how many individual orders have more than one item line on them, by grouping the item lines up to the order level first so no order is counted twice. No status filter is applied, so cancelled orders are included; ask if you'd like them excluded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customers.customer_unique_id) AS unique_customers FROM customers
explanation: This counts distinct people in the marketplace customer records, using the identifier that tracks a person across orders rather than the per-order customer record. Counting by the per-order identifier instead would overstate the base by about 3,345.

sql: SELECT customers.customer_state, COUNT(DISTINCT orders.order_id) AS order_count FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id WHERE orders.order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customers.customer_state ORDER BY order_count DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This counts distinct orders with a status of "delivered", grouped by the end customer's Brazilian state, and shows the five states with the highest counts. Only delivered orders are included, so shipped, cancelled and other statuses are excluded.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN orders.order_delivered_customer_date <= orders.order_estimated_delivery_date THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS on_time_delivery_rate FROM orders WHERE orders.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: This gives the share of orders that actually reached the customer on or before the promised delivery date. Orders with no delivery timestamp (never delivered) are left out rather than counted as late, so the figure describes delivered orders only.

sql: SELECT AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', orders.order_purchase_timestamp, orders.order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_delivery_days FROM orders WHERE orders.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: This gives the average number of days from when an order was purchased to when it reached the customer, across all marketplace orders. Orders with no recorded delivery date (about 2,965 of them) are left out rather than treated as very late, since their delivery time is unknown.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete
explanation: This counts signed clients whose first 90 days after signing fall entirely inside the commerce data, so their early revenue could actually be observed. Clients signed too late to have a full 90-day window are excluded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads WHERE funnel_leads.origin = 'not_recorded'
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads whose channel field was blank in the source data (labelled "not_recorded"). It deliberately excludes leads whose channel was recorded as "unknown" — that is a real recorded value meaning the source could not be identified, which is a different fact from having no entry at all.

sql: SELECT funnel_leads.origin AS channel, COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS conversion_rate, COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS leads, COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) AS deals FROM funnel_leads LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes ON deal_outcomes.mql_id = funnel_leads.mql_id GROUP BY funnel_leads.origin ORDER BY conversion_rate DESC
explanation: For each acquisition channel, this shows how many marketing-qualified leads it produced, how many of those became signed clients, and the resulting conversion share. All leads are included since becoming a deal is not affected by when the data ends. Note that 'unknown' means the source could not be identified, while 'not_recorded' means no source was recorded at all — they are kept separate.

The data records the state of the end customer on each order, but there is no state or location field for sellers anywhere in the layer — seller records carry only lifetime order and revenue figures, not geography. So revenue cannot be broken out by seller state without location data the layer does not hold.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.business_segment, COUNT(*) AS clients, AVG(CASE WHEN deal_outcomes.ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete GROUP BY deal_outcomes.business_segment HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 ORDER BY attachment_rate DESC
explanation: This shows, for each business segment, the share of signed clients that went on to bill any revenue, ranked highest first, and only for segments with at least twenty clients. It counts only deals that had a full 90-day observation window — a required filter, since deals signed near the end of the data cannot show revenue at all and would drag the rates down artificially.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT orders.order_id) AS cancelled_orders FROM orders WHERE orders.order_status = 'canceled'
explanation: This counts the distinct marketplace orders whose recorded status is "cancelled". No other filters are applied, so it covers the whole June 2017 – November 2018 data window.

sql: SELECT orders.order_status, AVG(order_reviews.review_score) AS avg_review_score, COUNT(*) AS review_rows FROM order_reviews JOIN orders ON order_reviews.order_id = orders.order_id GROUP BY orders.order_status ORDER BY avg_review_score DESC
explanation: This shows the mean customer review score (1 to 5) for orders grouped by their status, such as delivered, shipped or cancelled, along with how many reviews sit behind each figure. All statuses are included, so low-volume statuses like unavailable may rest on very few reviews.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.lead_type AS lead_type, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY deal_outcomes.lead_type ORDER BY deal_count DESC
explanation: This counts the signed clients in each lead-type classification (how the lead was categorised at qualification), from largest group to smallest. It covers all signed deals in the June 2017 to November 2018 window, with no revenue-window filter applied since this is a simple count rather than a rate.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(deal_outcomes.revenue_90d) AS median_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete AND deal_outcomes.ever_sold AND deal_outcomes.revenue_90d > 0
explanation: This shows the typical (middle) amount of revenue billed in the first 90 days after signing, counting only clients that actually billed something. It is restricted to clients who had a complete 90-day observation window — required, because clients signed near the end of the data could not yet show revenue.

The layer has no product category information. On the marketplace side, item lines carry only a product identifier, price and freight — no category name (English or Portuguese). The CRM product catalogue has product names and a product family (GTX, MG, GTK) with list prices, but nothing that corresponds to an "English category". Answering would need a product category table that isn't part of this layer.

sql: SELECT strftime(funnel_leads.first_contact_date, '%Y-%m') AS first_contact_month, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads by the calendar month of their first marketing contact, covering the whole observed period (June 2017 to November 2018). No filters are applied, so every qualified lead is included regardless of whether it later became a signed client.

sql: SELECT seller_id, revenue_brl, orders, avg_review_score FROM seller_performance ORDER BY revenue_brl DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This lists the five selling clients with the highest lifetime revenue, along with their order count and mean review score. Lifetime figures in this table already exclude cancelled orders. Sellers are shown by their anonymised identifier, as no names exist in the data.

sql: SELECT AVG(order_value) AS avg_order_value FROM (SELECT orders.order_id, SUM(order_items.price) AS order_value FROM order_items JOIN orders ON order_items.order_id = orders.order_id WHERE orders.order_status <> 'canceled' GROUP BY orders.order_id) t
explanation: This adds up the item prices within each order first, so an order with several lines is counted only once, then averages those order totals. Cancelled orders are excluded, and freight is not included since it is a pass-through cost rather than seller revenue.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS clients_no_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete AND NOT deal_outcomes.ever_sold
explanation: This counts signed clients who billed nothing in their first 90 days. It only includes clients who had a full 90-day observation window — clients signed too close to the end of the data are excluded, since they could not have shown revenue regardless.

sql: SELECT landing_page_id, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY landing_page_id ORDER BY lead_count DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads for each landing page and shows the five pages with the highest lead volume. It covers all qualified leads in the acquisition data (June 2017 to November 2018), with no filters applied.

sql: SELECT business_type, MEDIAN(days_to_close) AS median_days_to_close, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY business_type ORDER BY median_days_to_close
explanation: This shows, for each type of business signed, the typical number of days between the first marketing contact and the signature, along with how many signed clients fall in each type. We report the median rather than the mean because closing times are skewed and the median better represents a typical deal.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_reviews.order_id) AS orders_with_score_1 FROM order_reviews WHERE order_reviews.review_score = 1
explanation: This counts the distinct marketplace orders that received at least one one-star review. Because a single review record can be attached to more than one order, the count is taken over distinct orders rather than review rows.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_items.seller_id) AS distinct_sellers FROM order_items
explanation: This counts the number of different sellers that appear on at least one item line in the marketplace order data. No filters are applied, so it includes sellers whose only orders were later cancelled.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.lead_type, COUNT(*) AS deals, AVG(deal_outcomes.revenue_90d) AS avg_revenue_90d, MEDIAN(deal_outcomes.revenue_90d) AS median_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete GROUP BY deal_outcomes.lead_type ORDER BY avg_revenue_90d DESC
explanation: This shows, for each lead type, the average (and median) revenue that signed clients billed in their first 90 days. Only clients that had a full 90-day observation window are included — a required filter, since clients signed near the end of the data cannot show revenue by construction. Clients that never billed count as zero, which is a real outcome; the median is included because revenue is skewed.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.business_segment, SUM(deal_outcomes.revenue_90d) AS revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete GROUP BY deal_outcomes.business_segment ORDER BY revenue_90d DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This ranks the market segments of signed clients by the total revenue they billed in their first 90 days, showing the top five. Only clients that had a complete 90-day observation window are included — clients signed too late in the data to have a full window are excluded, since they cannot show revenue by construction.

sql: SELECT AVG(order_items.freight_value) AS avg_freight_per_item_line FROM order_items
explanation: This gives the average freight charge recorded on each individual item line across all marketplace order lines. Note it is per item line, not per order, and no filter for cancelled orders is applied since freight is not one of the governed revenue metrics — freight is a pass-through shipping charge, not seller revenue or a business cost measure.

sql: SELECT strftime(deal_outcomes.won_date, '%Y-%m') AS won_month, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: This counts signed clients by the month their deal was signed, across the whole acquisition window (June 2017 to November 2018). No filters are applied, so every signed client is included regardless of whether they later generated revenue.

sql: SELECT customers.customer_state, AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', orders.order_purchase_timestamp, orders.order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_delivery_days, COUNT(DISTINCT orders.order_id) AS delivered_orders FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id WHERE orders.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customers.customer_state HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT orders.order_id) >= 500 AND AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', orders.order_purchase_timestamp, orders.order_delivered_customer_date)) > 20 ORDER BY avg_delivery_days DESC
explanation: This lists Brazilian states where orders took, on average, more than 20 days from purchase to arrival at the customer, restricted to states with at least 500 delivered orders. Only orders that actually reached the customer are counted; orders with no delivery date are excluded, as delivery timing cannot be measured for them.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT order_items.order_id) AS avg_item_lines_per_order FROM order_items
explanation: This counts all item lines and divides by the number of distinct orders that have items, giving the average number of lines per order. It covers all orders present in the item data, including cancelled ones, since this is a count of lines rather than revenue.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE origin = 'paid_search') * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS paid_search_share, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE origin = 'paid_search') AS paid_search_deals, COUNT(*) AS total_deals FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This shows the share of all signed clients whose original marketing-qualified lead came through the paid search channel, alongside the counts behind it. It covers every signed deal in the acquisition data (June 2017–November 2018); no observation-window filter is needed since this is about lead source, not revenue outcomes.

sql: SELECT seller_id, reviews FROM seller_performance ORDER BY reviews DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5
explanation: This lists the five selling clients with the highest lifetime count of reviews, taken from the per-seller lifetime performance table (which already excludes cancelled orders). Sellers are shown by their anonymised identifier, as no names exist in the data.

sql: SELECT orders.order_status, COUNT(DISTINCT orders.order_id) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY orders.order_status ORDER BY order_count DESC
explanation: This counts the distinct marketplace orders in each status category (delivered, shipped, cancelled and so on), covering all orders in the data with no exclusions.

sql: SELECT SUM(deal_outcomes.revenue_90d) AS revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete
explanation: This sums the revenue billed by signed clients during their first 90 days, counting only clients who had a full 90-day observation window. That filter is essential: clients signed near the end of the data could not possibly show a full 90 days of revenue, so including them would understate the total.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.origin AS channel, AVG(CASE WHEN deal_outcomes.ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete GROUP BY deal_outcomes.origin ORDER BY attachment_rate DESC
explanation: For each acquisition channel, this shows the share of signed clients that went on to bill any revenue, along with how many such clients there were. Only clients with a full 90-day observation window are included, which is required — without that filter the rates are depressed simply because the commerce data ends before late-signed clients could sell. Channels with few deals will have noisy rates.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.behaviour_primary, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY deal_outcomes.behaviour_primary ORDER BY deal_count DESC
explanation: This counts signed clients by their recorded primary behaviour profile, ordered from most to least common. All signed clients are included, since this is a simple count and no observation-window filter is needed.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS sellers_below_3 FROM seller_performance WHERE avg_review_score < 3
explanation: This counts selling clients whose lifetime average review score is below 3 out of 5. Sellers with no reviews recorded have no score and are not counted.

sql: SELECT MAX(deal_outcomes.days_to_close) AS max_days_to_close FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This reports the largest number of days between a lead's first marketing contact and the date they signed, across all signed clients in the acquisition data. No filters applied, so it covers every signed client on record.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This counts every sales opportunity in the CRM pipeline, whether still open (Prospecting, Engaging) or already closed (Won, Lost). No filters applied.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS account_count FROM crm_accounts
explanation: This counts every client company listed in the CRM account list (one row per account). It covers the sales-pipeline dataset only, with no filters applied.

sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN is_won THEN close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This adds up the closing value of every opportunity marked as won in the 2017 sales pipeline. Lost deals (value zero) and still-open deals contribute nothing to the total.

sql: SELECT series, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM crm_products GROUP BY series ORDER BY product_count DESC
explanation: This counts how many products in the catalogue belong to each product family (series). No filters applied — the full catalogue is included.

sql: SELECT deal_stage, COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY deal_stage ORDER BY opportunity_count DESC
explanation: This counts every sales opportunity in the CRM pipeline, grouped by its stage (Prospecting, Engaging, Won, Lost). No filters are applied, so both open and closed opportunities are included.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN is_won THEN close_value END) AS avg_won_value FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This gives the average close value across opportunities that were won in the 2017 sales pipeline. Lost and still-open deals are skipped entirely rather than counted as zero, which would otherwise pull the average down.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_closed
explanation: This gives the share of closed sales opportunities that were won. Only closed deals are counted — still-open opportunities are excluded because their outcome isn't known yet, and counting them would understate the rate.

sql: SELECT sales_agent, SUM(CASE WHEN is_won THEN close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY sales_agent ORDER BY booked_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This ranks sales agents by the total value of the deals they won in the 2017 pipeline, showing the top five. Lost and still-open opportunities contribute nothing to the total.

sql: SELECT a.sector, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate, COUNT(*) AS closed_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON a.account = o.account WHERE o.is_closed GROUP BY a.sector ORDER BY win_rate DESC
explanation: This shows, for each industry sector of the client accounts, the share of decided (closed) opportunities that were won. Open deals are excluded because their outcome is not yet known, and opportunities with no named account are excluded by the join. Differences between sectors here are typically within sampling noise, so the closed-deal counts are shown alongside for context.

sql: SELECT manager, COUNT(DISTINCT sales_agent) AS agents FROM crm_sales_teams GROUP BY manager ORDER BY agents DESC
explanation: This counts how many distinct sales agents are listed under each manager in the sales team roster. No filters are applied, so it covers the full team list.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(cycle_days) AS median_cycle_days FROM crm_opportunities WHERE cycle_days IS NOT NULL AND is_won
explanation: This gives the typical (median) number of days from engaging a prospect to closing, counting only opportunities that were won. Deals with no recorded cycle length (such as those still in Prospecting, which never had an engagement date) are excluded. The median is used because deal cycle lengths are unevenly spread and an average would describe no real deal.

sql: SELECT product, series, list_price FROM crm_products WHERE list_price > 3000 ORDER BY list_price DESC
explanation: This lists every product in the sales catalogue whose list price is above 3,000, along with its product family, from highest price down. It uses the catalogue only, so no deal activity is involved.

sql: SELECT t.regional_office, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = o.sales_agent GROUP BY t.regional_office ORDER BY booked_value DESC
explanation: This totals the value of won deals for each regional office, based on the office of the agent who owned the opportunity. Lost and still-open opportunities contribute nothing to the total. Figures come from the synthetic 2017 sales pipeline dataset.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities WHERE account IS NULL OR TRIM(account) = ''
explanation: This counts sales pipeline opportunities that name no client account (either blank or missing). These rows are the ones excluded from any account-level analysis.

sql: SELECT strftime(won_date, '%Y-%m') AS won_month, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes WHERE won_date >= DATE '2017-01-01' AND won_date < DATE '2018-01-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: This counts signed clients (closed deals) by the month their deal was signed, limited to 2017. Note the acquisition data begins in June 2017, so earlier months of 2017 will show no deals.

sql: SELECT p.series AS product_series, MEDIAN(o.close_value) AS median_won_value, COUNT(*) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_products p ON p.product = o.product WHERE o.is_won GROUP BY p.series ORDER BY median_won_value DESC
explanation: This shows the middle (median) value of won deals within each product family (GTX, MG, GTK), along with how many won deals sit behind each figure. Only deals actually marked as won are counted, so lost deals (recorded as zero value) and still-open deals do not distort the numbers. Note this is synthetic sales-pipeline data for a fictitious vendor.

sql: SELECT account, employees, office_location, revenue_musd, year_established FROM crm_accounts WHERE sector = 'technology' AND employees > 5000 ORDER BY employees DESC
explanation: This lists client accounts recorded in the technology sector with a headcount above 5,000, showing size, location, revenue and founding year. It is a simple lookup of the account list from the sales pipeline dataset, with no filtering on deals.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN is_closed THEN 0.0 ELSE 1.0 END) AS open_share, COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This gives the share of all sales opportunities in the pipeline that are not yet closed (i.e. still in Prospecting or Engaging), alongside the total opportunity count. No filters applied — all opportunities are included, since the question is about the whole pipeline.

sql: SELECT t.manager, COUNT(*) AS closed_opportunities, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won_opportunities, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = o.sales_agent WHERE o.is_closed GROUP BY t.manager ORDER BY closed_opportunities DESC
explanation: For each manager's team, this counts the opportunities that reached a final outcome (won or lost) and how many of those were won, plus the resulting win rate. Open deals still in Prospecting or Engaging are excluded because their outcome isn't known yet. Differences in win rate between managers in this teaching dataset are small enough to be within sampling noise.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS subsidiary_accounts FROM crm_accounts WHERE parent_account IS NOT NULL
explanation: This counts client accounts in the sales pipeline dataset that have a parent company recorded, i.e. subsidiaries. Accounts with no parent listed are treated as standalone.

sql: SELECT a.sector, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value END) AS avg_won_value, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE o.is_won) AS won_deals FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON a.account = o.account GROUP BY a.sector HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE o.is_won) > 0 ORDER BY avg_won_value DESC
explanation: This ranks client sectors by the average value of deals that were actually won; lost and still-open opportunities are excluded from the average rather than counted as zero. Opportunities that name no account cannot be assigned a sector, so they are left out. The top row is the answer, with the number of won deals shown so you can judge how thin the evidence is.

sql: SELECT SUM(p.list_price) AS open_pipeline_list_value, COUNT(*) AS open_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_products p ON p.product = o.product WHERE NOT o.is_closed
explanation: This adds up the catalogue list price of the product attached to each still-open opportunity (those in Prospecting or Engaging, i.e. not closed), giving the list-price value of the open pipeline. It is not a forecast of bookings: won deals often close above or below list price, and open deals have no close value recorded yet.

sql: SELECT o.account, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities o WHERE o.account IS NOT NULL GROUP BY o.account ORDER BY booked_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This ranks client accounts in the sales pipeline by the total value of deals actually won; lost and still-open deals contribute nothing. Opportunities that name no account (1,425 of them) are excluded, since they cannot be attributed to a client.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads
explanation: This counts every marketing-qualified lead recorded in the acquisition funnel, with no filters applied.

sql: SELECT deal_stage, MEDIAN(cycle_days) AS median_cycle_days, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM crm_opportunities WHERE cycle_days IS NOT NULL AND deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost') GROUP BY deal_stage ORDER BY deal_stage
explanation: This shows the typical (median) number of days from engagement to close, separately for won and lost opportunities in the 2017 sales pipeline. Opportunities without a recorded cycle length (all still-prospecting deals) are excluded, since their cycle time does not exist yet. Medians are used because deal durations are skewed.

sql: SELECT origin AS channel, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY origin ORDER BY lead_count DESC
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads by the channel that produced them. Note that "unknown" means the source could not be identified, while "not_recorded" means no source was captured at all — they are kept separate rather than combined.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) AS signed_clients, COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS leads, COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS conversion_rate FROM funnel_leads LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes ON deal_outcomes.mql_id = funnel_leads.mql_id
explanation: This counts how many marketing-qualified leads there were in total, how many of them went on to sign as clients, and the resulting conversion share. All leads are included, since whether a lead converts is fully observed in this data.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT d.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT l.mql_id) AS conversion_rate FROM funnel_leads l LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes d ON d.mql_id = l.mql_id
explanation: This gives the share of all marketing-qualified leads that went on to become signed clients, over the whole June 2017 – November 2018 window. No observation-window filter is needed here, because whether a lead signed is fully recorded for every lead.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete
explanation: This measures the share of signed clients that went on to bill any revenue. It counts only clients who had a full 90-day observation window; without that filter the figure would be artificially low simply because the commerce data ends before late-signing clients could sell.

sql: SELECT business_segment, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY business_segment ORDER BY deal_count DESC LIMIT 10
explanation: This counts signed clients (closed deals) grouped by the market segment they sell into, showing the ten largest segments. All signed clients are included regardless of whether they later generated revenue, so no observation-window filter is needed.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(deal_outcomes.days_to_close) AS median_days_to_close FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This gives the typical (median) number of days between a lead's first marketing contact and the date the client signed, across all signed clients. The median is used rather than the average because a few very long courtships would distort a mean. No observation-window filter is needed here, since the signing date is known for every deal.

sql: SELECT origin AS channel, SUM(revenue_90d) AS revenue_90d, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY origin ORDER BY revenue_90d DESC
explanation: This totals the revenue that newly signed clients billed within 90 days of signing, split by the acquisition channel that produced the lead. Only deals with a complete 90-day observation window are included — deals signed too close to the end of the data cannot show revenue, and including them would understate the totals.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count FROM orders
explanation: This counts every distinct order in the marketplace data, including cancelled and undelivered ones. If you want only live orders, cancelled ones would need to be excluded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_with_multiple_lines FROM (SELECT order_id FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) t
explanation: This counts how many orders have two or more item lines, by grouping item lines up to the order level first so no order is counted twice. It includes orders of every status, since the question is about basket composition rather than revenue.

sql: SELECT SUM(i.price) AS order_revenue FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id WHERE o.order_status <> 'canceled'
explanation: This totals the item prices on every order that was not cancelled. It excludes freight, which is a pass-through cost rather than seller revenue, and excludes cancelled orders as required.

sql: SELECT AVG(review_score) AS avg_review_score FROM order_reviews
explanation: This gives the mean customer review score, on a 1-to-5 scale, across all reviews in the marketplace data. No filters are applied, so every recorded review is included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_unique_id) AS unique_customers FROM customers
explanation: This counts distinct people in the marketplace customer records. It uses the person-level identifier rather than the per-order customer record, which would overstate the customer base by about 3,345.

sql: SELECT c.customer_state, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY c.customer_state ORDER BY order_count DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This counts distinct orders with a status of "delivered" and groups them by the end customer's Brazilian state, showing the top five. Only delivered orders are included, so shipped, cancelled or unavailable orders are excluded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS deals_with_complete_window FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete
explanation: This counts the signed clients whose first 90 days after signing fall entirely inside the observed commerce data, so their early revenue could actually be measured. Clients signed too late in the period to have a full 90 days are excluded.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN orders.order_delivered_customer_date <= orders.order_estimated_delivery_date THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS on_time_delivery_rate FROM orders WHERE orders.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: This gives the share of orders that actually reached the customer on or before the promised delivery date. Orders with no delivery timestamp (never delivered) are excluded rather than counted as late, so the figure describes delivered orders only.

sql: SELECT AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', orders.order_purchase_timestamp, orders.order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_delivery_days FROM orders WHERE orders.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: This gives the average number of days from when an order was purchased to when the customer received it. Only orders with a recorded delivery date are included — orders never delivered (or missing that timestamp) are left out rather than counted as very late.

The layer records state only for end customers (customer_state), not for sellers. Seller records carry lifetime orders, revenue and review scores, but no location, so revenue cannot be broken out by seller state. Answering would need seller geography data the layer does not hold.

sql: SELECT l.origin AS channel, COUNT(DISTINCT d.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT l.mql_id) AS conversion_rate, COUNT(DISTINCT l.mql_id) AS leads, COUNT(DISTINCT d.mql_id) AS deals FROM funnel_leads l LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes d ON d.mql_id = l.mql_id GROUP BY l.origin ORDER BY conversion_rate DESC
explanation: For each acquisition channel, this shows how many marketing-qualified leads there were, how many became signed clients, and the share that converted. It uses every lead, since whether a lead signs is not affected by when the data ends. Note that 'unknown' means the source could not be identified while 'not_recorded' means no source was captured — they are kept separate.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads WHERE origin = 'not_recorded'
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads whose acquisition channel field was empty in the source, labelled 'not_recorded'. It deliberately excludes leads recorded as 'unknown', which means the source was investigated but could not be identified — a different fact.

sql: SELECT business_segment, COUNT(*) AS clients, AVG(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY business_segment HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 ORDER BY attachment_rate DESC
explanation: This shows, for each market segment a signed client sells into, the share of those clients who went on to bill any revenue, limited to segments with at least twenty clients. Only clients that had a full 90-day observation window are included — that filter is required, since clients signed near the end of the data could not yet show revenue.

sql: SELECT lead_type, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY lead_type ORDER BY deal_count DESC
explanation: This counts the signed clients in the acquisition funnel, broken down by the lead type recorded when the lead was qualified. All signed deals are included, with no time or observation-window restriction, since this is a simple count rather than a rate or revenue figure.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS cancelled_orders FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'canceled'
explanation: This counts the distinct marketplace orders whose status is recorded as cancelled. No other filters applied, so it covers the whole June 2017 to November 2018 window.
