sql: SELECT MEDIAN(revenue_90d) AS median_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete AND ever_sold AND revenue_90d > 0
explanation: This gives the typical (median) revenue billed in the first 90 days after signing, counting only signed clients that actually billed something. It is restricted to deals that had a full 90-day observation window, which is required — otherwise clients signed near the end of the data would look like they earned nothing.

sql: SELECT o.order_status, AVG(r.review_score) AS avg_review_score, COUNT(*) AS reviews FROM order_reviews r JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = r.order_id GROUP BY o.order_status ORDER BY avg_review_score DESC
explanation: This shows the mean review score (1 to 5) given on orders, broken out by the order's status, along with how many reviews sit behind each figure. All statuses including cancelled are shown, since the question asks about each status; small groups may rest on very few reviews.

sql: SELECT strftime(first_contact_date, '%Y-%m') AS first_contact_month, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads by the month of their first contact, across the whole acquisition dataset (June 2017 to November 2018). No filters are applied, so every qualified lead is included regardless of whether it later became a signed client.

The layer has no product category information for the marketplace data — order item lines carry only a product identifier, price and freight, with no category name (English or Portuguese). The CRM product catalogue has product names and series, but no "English category". Answering would need a product category table that is not part of this layer.

sql: SELECT seller_id, revenue_brl, orders, avg_review_score FROM seller_performance ORDER BY revenue_brl DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This lists the five selling clients with the largest lifetime revenue, alongside their order count and mean review score. Lifetime figures in this table already exclude cancelled orders. Sellers are identified only by anonymised IDs.

sql: SELECT AVG(order_total) AS avg_order_value FROM (SELECT i.order_id, SUM(i.price) AS order_total FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id WHERE o.order_status <> 'canceled' GROUP BY i.order_id) t
explanation: This totals the item prices within each order first, so an order with several lines counts only once, then averages those order totals. Cancelled orders are excluded, and freight is not counted as revenue.

sql: SELECT landing_page_id, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY landing_page_id ORDER BY lead_count DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads by the landing page that produced them, and shows the five landing pages with the highest lead volume. No filters applied — all qualified leads are included.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS clients_no_revenue FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete AND NOT ever_sold
explanation: This counts signed clients who billed nothing in their first 90 days. Only clients with a full 90-day observation window are included; deals signed too late to be observed are excluded, since they cannot show revenue by construction.

sql: SELECT business_type, MEDIAN(days_to_close) AS median_days_to_close, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY business_type ORDER BY median_days_to_close
explanation: This shows, for each type of business among signed clients, the typical number of days between first marketing contact and signature, along with how many deals sit behind each figure. The median is used rather than the average because closing times are heavily skewed and an average would describe no real deal.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS n FROM order_reviews WHERE review_score = 1
explanation: This counts the distinct orders that received a one-star review. Orders are counted once even if more than one review row attaches to them, since review records are not unique per order.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT seller_id) AS distinct_sellers FROM order_items
explanation: This counts how many different sellers appear across all item lines in the marketplace order data. No filters are applied, so it includes sellers on cancelled orders as well.

sql: SELECT AVG(freight_value) AS avg_freight_per_item_line FROM order_items
explanation: This gives the average freight charge recorded on a single item line across all item lines in the marketplace data. Note it covers every line regardless of order status (cancelled orders included), and freight is a shipping charge, not a profit or cost measure.

sql: SELECT business_segment, SUM(revenue_90d) AS revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY business_segment ORDER BY revenue_90d DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This totals the revenue signed clients billed in their first 90 days, grouped by the market segment they sell into, showing the top five. Only deals with a complete 90-day observation window are included — deals signed too close to the end of the data cannot show revenue, so including them would understate the figures.

sql: SELECT lead_type, COUNT(*) AS deals, AVG(revenue_90d) AS avg_revenue_90d, MEDIAN(revenue_90d) AS median_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY lead_type ORDER BY avg_revenue_90d DESC
explanation: This shows, for each lead type, the average revenue signed clients billed in their first 90 days, along with the number of clients and the median (revenue is skewed, so the median is often the more representative figure). Only clients who had a full 90-day observation window are included — required, because clients signed near the end of the data could not yet show revenue. Clients that never billed count as zero, which is a real outcome.

sql: SELECT strftime(won_date, '%Y-%m') AS won_month, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY won_month ORDER BY won_month
explanation: This counts signed clients (closed deals) by the month they signed, across the whole acquisition window (June 2017 to November 2018). No revenue or rate is involved, so no observation-window filter is needed.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN origin = 'paid_search' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS paid_search_share, COUNT(*) AS total_deals FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This gives the share of all signed clients whose originating acquisition channel was recorded as paid search, alongside the total number of signed clients. It covers every signed client, since channel attribution is not affected by the 90-day revenue observation window.

sql: SELECT c.customer_state, AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', o.order_purchase_timestamp, o.order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_delivery_days, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS delivered_orders FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c.customer_state HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) >= 500 AND AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', o.order_purchase_timestamp, o.order_delivered_customer_date)) > 20 ORDER BY avg_delivery_days DESC
explanation: This lists Brazilian states where orders took on average more than 20 days from purchase to arrival, restricted to states with at least 500 orders that actually reached the customer. Orders with no delivery date recorded are excluded rather than treated as late, so the figure describes completed deliveries only.

sql: SELECT seller_id, reviews FROM seller_performance ORDER BY reviews DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5
explanation: This lists the five selling clients with the highest lifetime count of reviews, taken from the per-seller lifetime performance table (which already excludes cancelled orders). Sellers are shown by their anonymised identifier, as no names exist in the data.

sql: SELECT AVG(lines) AS avg_item_lines_per_order FROM (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS lines FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id)
explanation: This counts the item lines on each order first, then averages across orders, so a single order with several lines is counted once. It covers all orders that have item lines, without excluding cancelled ones, since no revenue figure is involved.

sql: SELECT order_status, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY order_status ORDER BY order_count DESC
explanation: This counts the marketplace orders in each status category (delivered, shipped, cancelled, and so on). No filters applied — cancelled orders are included here because the question asks for a breakdown by status.

sql: SELECT origin AS channel, AVG(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY origin ORDER BY attachment_rate DESC
explanation: For each acquisition channel, this shows the share of signed clients that went on to bill any revenue, along with how many signed clients sit behind each figure. Only clients with a full 90-day observation window are included, which is required — without that filter the rates are artificially low because the commerce data ends before late-signed deals could bill. Channels with few deals will have noisy rates.

sql: SELECT SUM(revenue_90d) AS revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete
explanation: This adds up the revenue billed by signed clients during their first 90 days after signing. Only clients that had a full 90-day observation window are included — this filter is required, since clients signed near the end of the data could not yet show revenue.

sql: SELECT behaviour_primary, COUNT(*) AS deals FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY behaviour_primary ORDER BY deals DESC
explanation: This counts signed clients by their primary behaviour profile, listing the most common first. It covers all signed clients, with no 90-day observation window filter, since this is a simple count rather than a revenue or rate measure.

sql: SELECT MAX(days_to_close) AS max_days_to_close FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This reports the largest number of days between a lead's first marketing contact and the date the client signed, across all signed clients. No filters are applied, since this is a simple maximum rather than a rate or revenue figure.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS sellers_below_3 FROM seller_performance WHERE avg_review_score < 3
explanation: This counts selling clients whose lifetime average customer review score is below 3 out of 5. It covers only sellers that actually listed and sold (those present in the seller performance table), and their scores are based on non-cancelled orders. Sellers with no reviews recorded are not counted.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_opportunities FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_closed = false
explanation: This counts all opportunities in crm_opportunities that are not yet closed (i.e., still active in the sales pipeline), giving the total number of open deals currently being tracked.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT account) AS client_account_count FROM crm_accounts
explanation: This counts the distinct number of client accounts listed in the CRM accounts table.

sql: SELECT series, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM crm_products GROUP BY series ORDER BY product_count DESC
explanation: This counts the number of products in the crm_products table grouped by their series, showing how many products belong to each series.

sql: SELECT deal_stage, COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY deal_stage ORDER BY opportunity_count DESC
explanation: This counts the number of opportunities grouped by their deal stage (e.g., Won, Lost, Engaging), showing how many opportunities are currently at each stage of the sales pipeline.

sql: SELECT SUM(close_value) AS total_won_value FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won = true
explanation: This sums the close_value field for all opportunities marked as won (is_won = true) in the CRM opportunities table, giving the total dollar value of all successfully closed deals.

sql: SELECT AVG(close_value) AS avg_won_deal_value FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won = true
explanation: This calculates the average close_value of all opportunities marked as won in the CRM opportunities table.

sql: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DOUBLE) / COUNT(*) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_closed
explanation: This calculates the percentage of closed deals that were won, by dividing the count of won deals by the total count of closed deals in the CRM opportunities table.

sql:
SELECT sales_agent, SUM(close_value) AS total_close_value
FROM crm_opportunities
WHERE is_won = true
GROUP BY sales_agent
ORDER BY total_close_value DESC
LIMIT 5
explanation: This sums the close value of won deals for each sales agent and returns the five agents with the highest total booked value.

sql: SELECT a.sector, COUNT(*) AS total_opportunities, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won_opportunities, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON o.account = a.account WHERE o.is_closed GROUP BY a.sector ORDER BY win_rate DESC
explanation: This measures, for each client's sector, the share of closed opportunities that were won (won deals divided by all closed deals). Only closed opportunities are counted since win/loss is only determined once a deal is closed.

sql: SELECT median(cycle_days) AS median_sales_cycle_days FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won = true
explanation: This calculates the median value of the cycle_days field (the sales cycle length) for all opportunities marked as won, giving a typical sales cycle duration that is less affected by outliers than an average.

sql:
SELECT t.regional_office, SUM(o.close_value) AS booked_value
FROM crm_opportunities o
JOIN crm_sales_teams t ON o.sales_agent = t.sales_agent
WHERE o.is_won = true
GROUP BY t.regional_office
ORDER BY booked_value DESC
explanation: This sums the close value of all won opportunities, joined to sales agents' regional offices, to show total booked (won) deal value per regional office.

sql: SELECT manager, COUNT(DISTINCT sales_agent) AS num_agents FROM crm_sales_teams GROUP BY manager ORDER BY num_agents DESC
explanation: Counts the number of distinct sales agents associated with each manager in the sales teams table.

sql: SELECT product, list_price FROM crm_products WHERE list_price > 3000 ORDER BY list_price DESC
explanation: This lists all products from the CRM product catalog whose list price exceeds 3000, sorted from highest to lowest price.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunities_without_account FROM crm_opportunities WHERE account IS NULL
explanation: This counts the number of rows in the CRM opportunities table where the account field is empty (NULL), meaning the opportunity has no associated account recorded.

sql:
SELECT p.series, MEDIAN(o.close_value) AS median_won_deal_value
FROM crm_opportunities o
JOIN crm_products p ON o.product = p.product
WHERE o.is_won = true
GROUP BY p.series
ORDER BY p.series
explanation: This calculates the median close_value of won opportunities (is_won = true), grouped by the product series they belong to (joining crm_opportunities to crm_products on product name).

sql:
SELECT strftime(close_date, '%Y-%m') AS close_month, COUNT(*) AS deals_closed
FROM crm_opportunities
WHERE is_closed = true AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM close_date) = 2017
GROUP BY close_month
ORDER BY close_month
explanation: This counts the number of closed deals (deal_stage marked as closed) in the crm_opportunities table, grouped by month for the year 2017, based on the close_date field.

sql: SELECT account, employees, sector FROM crm_accounts WHERE sector = 'technology' AND employees > 5000
explanation: This lists all accounts from the CRM accounts table whose sector is 'technology' and whose employee count exceeds 5000.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN is_closed = 0 OR is_closed = false THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS share_open FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This calculates the percentage of opportunities in the CRM data where the is_closed flag indicates the deal has not yet been closed (won or lost), representing the share of deals still open/in progress.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS subsidiary_accounts FROM crm_accounts WHERE parent_account IS NOT NULL
explanation: Counts the number of rows in crm_accounts where the parent_account field is populated, indicating the account is a subsidiary of another company.

sql:
SELECT a.sector, AVG(o.close_value) AS avg_won_deal_value
FROM crm_opportunities o
JOIN crm_accounts a ON o.account = a.account
WHERE o.is_won = true
GROUP BY a.sector
ORDER BY avg_won_deal_value DESC
LIMIT 1

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT mql_id) AS mql_count FROM funnel_leads

sql: SELECT origin, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY origin ORDER BY lead_count DESC

sql: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DOUBLE) / COUNT(*) AS conversion_share FROM deal_outcomes

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders FROM orders

sql:

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT order_id FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) t

sql: SELECT AVG(review_score) AS avg_review_score FROM order_reviews

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_unique_id) AS unique_customers FROM customers

explanation: This counts the number of orders in the orders table grouped by their order_status value, showing how many orders fall into each status category (e.g., delivered, shipped, canceled).

sql: SELECT SUM(revenue_90d) AS total_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete = true

sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN is_won THEN close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities

explanation: This counts the number of sellers in the marketplace whose average review score across all their orders falls below 3 on the 1-5 scale.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This query counts all opportunities in the CRM pipeline, whether they are open or closed. It includes opportunities at every stage: Prospecting, Engaging, Won, and Lost.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS client_accounts FROM crm_accounts
explanation: This counts the total number of client accounts in the CRM dataset. Each row in the crm_accounts table represents one account company.

sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN crm_opportunities.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS total_value FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This sums the close_value of all opportunities marked as won. Lost and open opportunities contribute nothing to this total.

sql: SELECT series, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM crm_products GROUP BY series ORDER BY product_count DESC
explanation: This query counts the number of individual products in the catalog grouped by product series. Each row in the products table represents one product, so a simple count by series gives us the size of each product family.

sql: SELECT deal_stage, COUNT(*) AS opportunity_count FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY deal_stage ORDER BY opportunity_count DESC
explanation: This query counts the total number of opportunities in each sales pipeline stage (Prospecting, Engaging, Won, or Lost). Every opportunity in the dataset is included, whether currently open or already closed.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities WHERE crm_opportunities.is_closed
explanation: This query measures the share of closed opportunities that were won, excluding open deals whose outcomes are not yet known. The result is a percentage between 0 and 1 representing how many closed deals resulted in a win.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN crm_opportunities.is_won THEN crm_opportunities.close_value END) AS avg_won_value FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This measures the mean value of opportunities that closed as won. Only won deals are included in the average; lost and open deals are excluded from the calculation.

sql: SELECT sales_agent, SUM(CASE WHEN is_won THEN close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities GROUP BY sales_agent ORDER BY booked_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This query ranks sales agents by the total value of their won deals, showing the top five. Booked value counts only won opportunities; lost and open deals contribute nothing.

sql: SELECT ca.sector, AVG(CASE WHEN co.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities co LEFT JOIN crm_accounts ca ON co.account = ca.account WHERE co.is_closed AND ca.sector IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ca.sector ORDER BY win_rate DESC
explanation: This query calculates the share of closed opportunities that were won, broken down by client sector. Only closed opportunities are included (as required by the win_rate metric), and sectors are grouped to show performance differences across industries. Opportunities without an assigned account or sector are excluded.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(cycle_days) AS median_cycle_days FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_won AND cycle_days IS NOT NULL
explanation: This query measures the median number of days from engagement to close for deals that were won. Only deals with a defined cycle time are included, which excludes Prospecting stage opportunities that have no engagement date yet.

sql: SELECT manager, COUNT(*) AS agent_count FROM crm_sales_teams GROUP BY manager ORDER BY agent_count DESC
explanation: This query counts the number of sales agents in the crm_sales_teams table who report to each manager. It groups the data by manager and sorts the results by the count in descending order to show which managers oversee the most agents.

sql: SELECT st.regional_office, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_sales_teams st ON o.sales_agent = st.sales_agent GROUP BY st.regional_office ORDER BY booked_value DESC
explanation: This query shows the total value of won deals, grouped by the regional office of the sales agent who closed them. The booked value includes only won opportunities; lost and open deals contribute nothing.

sql: SELECT product, list_price FROM crm_products WHERE list_price > 3000 ORDER BY list_price DESC
explanation: This query identifies all products in the catalogue with a list price exceeding 3000, ordered from highest to lowest price. No aggregation or metric is applied—it's a simple filter on the product price dimension.

sql: SELECT strftime(close_date, '%Y-%m') AS close_month, COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM crm_opportunities WHERE is_closed AND strftime(close_date, '%Y') = '2017' GROUP BY strftime(close_date, '%Y-%m') ORDER BY close_month
explanation: This query counts the number of opportunities that closed (both won and lost) in each month of 2017. We filter to closed deals only and group by month to show how many deals closed each month.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS opportunities_with_no_account FROM crm_opportunities WHERE account IS NULL
explanation: This counts opportunities in the CRM pipeline where the account field is null or blank. The data documentation notes that 1,425 opportunities name no account, and any account-level analysis must exclude them.

sql: SELECT crm_products.series, MEDIAN(crm_opportunities.close_value) AS median_won_value FROM crm_opportunities JOIN crm_products ON crm_opportunities.product = crm_products.product WHERE crm_opportunities.is_won GROUP BY crm_products.series ORDER BY median_won_value DESC
explanation: This query calculates the median close value for opportunities that were won, grouped by product series. The median is used rather than the mean because deal values are often skewed. Only won deals are included, excluding lost and open opportunities.

sql: SELECT account, employees FROM crm_accounts WHERE sector = 'Technology' AND employees > 5000 ORDER BY employees DESC
explanation: This query returns all client accounts in the Technology sector that have more than 5,000 employees. It shows the account name and employee count for each match.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN is_closed THEN 0.0 ELSE 1.0 END) AS share_open FROM crm_opportunities
explanation: This calculates the share of all opportunities in the pipeline that have not yet closed. It includes opportunities at every stage: Prospecting, Engaging, Won, and Lost, then measures what fraction remain open.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM crm_accounts WHERE parent_account IS NOT NULL
explanation: This counts the number of accounts in the CRM system that have a parent account recorded, indicating they are subsidiaries or child entities of another company.

sql: SELECT st.manager, COUNT(*) AS opportunities_closed, SUM(CASE WHEN co.is_won THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS opportunities_won FROM crm_opportunities co JOIN crm_sales_teams st ON co.sales_agent = st.sales_agent WHERE co.is_closed GROUP BY st.manager ORDER BY opportunities_closed DESC
explanation: This query counts closed opportunities (both won and lost) by manager, and also counts how many of those closed opportunities were won. Each manager's team is identified through the sales agent who owns each opportunity.

sql: SELECT a.sector, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value END) AS avg_won_value FROM crm_opportunities o LEFT JOIN crm_accounts a ON o.account = a.account WHERE o.account IS NOT NULL GROUP BY a.sector ORDER BY avg_won_value DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: This query finds the sector with the highest average value of won deals. It uses the avg_won_value metric definition, which averages the close_value only for opportunities marked as won, excluding lost and open deals. Opportunities without an associated account (1,425 of them) are excluded from the analysis.

sql: SELECT SUM(crm_products.list_price * crm_opportunities.close_value) AS total_list_price_value FROM crm_opportunities JOIN crm_products ON crm_opportunities.product = crm_products.product WHERE crm_opportunities.is_closed = FALSE
explanation: This query sums the list price of products across all open opportunities (deals not yet closed). It multiplies each product's list price by the opportunity's close value to get the total value represented in the pipeline. Open deals have NULL close_value rather than a number, so this will return NULL.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads
explanation: This counts the total number of marketing-qualified leads in the acquisition funnel dataset. These are leads that passed marketing qualification between June 2017 and November 2018.

sql: SELECT a.account, SUM(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN o.close_value ELSE 0 END) AS booked_value FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON o.account = a.account WHERE o.account IS NOT NULL GROUP BY a.account ORDER BY booked_value DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This query identifies the five accounts with the highest total value of won deals. Booked value is the sum of close values from opportunities marked as won; lost and open opportunities contribute nothing. The query excludes the 1,425 opportunities with no account name.

Cycle length is defined only for opportunities that have been engaged (have an engage_date). By construction, every Prospecting opportunity lacks an engage_date, so cycle_days is undefined for them. Lost deals span all stages including Prospecting, many of which have no cycle_days value. The metric median_cycle_days requires filtering to opportunities where cycle_days IS NOT NULL, but this filter excludes most lost deals at the Prospecting stage, making the comparison between won and lost deals incomplete and misleading. A comparison of cycle time between won and lost deals would need to exclude Prospecting-stage deals from both groups to be honest, which changes the question from "won vs lost" to "engaged deals: won vs lost".

sql: SELECT origin, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY origin ORDER BY lead_count DESC
explanation: This counts the number of marketing-qualified leads by their acquisition channel (origin). Each row represents a distinct lead that passed marketing qualification, grouped by the channel that produced them.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) AS signed_clients FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This counts the distinct marketing-qualified leads that appear in the deal_outcomes table, meaning they converted from leads into signed clients. Each lead is counted once regardless of how many orders they later placed.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS conversion_rate FROM funnel_leads LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes ON funnel_leads.mql_id = deal_outcomes.mql_id
explanation: This measures the share of marketing-qualified leads that went on to sign a deal and become clients. The calculation counts distinct leads that converted (signed a deal) divided by the total number of distinct marketing-qualified leads, regardless of outcome.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete
explanation: This query measures the share of signed clients that generated any revenue, using the mandatory filter on window_complete. This filter ensures we only count clients with a full 90-day observation window, excluding deals signed late in the data period when revenue could not be fully observed.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(days_to_close) AS median_days_to_close FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This measures the median number of days from a lead's first marketing contact to the date they signed as a client. It answers your question about the typical sales cycle length in the acquisition funnel.

sql: SELECT business_segment, COUNT(*) AS signed_clients FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY business_segment ORDER BY signed_clients DESC LIMIT 10
explanation: This counts the number of signed clients (deals) in each business segment and shows the top ten by volume. Each row in deal_outcomes represents one signed client, so a simple count by segment provides the answer.

sql: SELECT origin AS channel, SUM(revenue_90d) AS revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY origin ORDER BY revenue_90d DESC
explanation: This query shows the total revenue billed by signed clients in their first 90 days after signing, grouped by the marketing channel that brought them in. It includes only deals with a complete 90-day observation window, meaning they closed early enough to have a full 90 days of data; deals signed late in the observation period are excluded because their revenue window would be cut off by the data end date.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS total_orders FROM orders
explanation: This query counts the distinct number of orders in the acquisition dataset. We count each order once even if it contains multiple item lines.

sql: SELECT SUM(order_items.price) AS total_item_revenue FROM order_items JOIN orders ON orders.order_id = order_items.order_id WHERE orders.order_status <> 'canceled'
explanation: This query sums the item-level prices across all orders that have not been cancelled. It excludes cancelled orders and freight costs, measuring only the seller revenue from items sold.

sql: SELECT AVG(review_score) AS avg_review_score FROM order_reviews
explanation: This query calculates the mean review score across all reviews left by customers on the Olist marketplace. Review scores range from 1 to 5.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_with_multiple_lines FROM (SELECT order_id FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)
explanation: This counts the number of distinct orders that contain more than one item line. Each row in order_items represents a single item line within an order, so we group by order_id and count lines per order, keeping only those with more than one line.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_unique_id) AS unique_customers FROM customers
explanation: This counts the number of unique people who placed orders on the marketplace. Each customer_unique_id represents a distinct person, regardless of how many separate order records they may have generated.

sql: SELECT customer_state, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS delivered_orders FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_state ORDER BY delivered_orders DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This query counts the distinct delivered orders by the state where the customer is located, grouped by state and ordered from highest to lowest. We filter to only orders with a status of 'delivered' to focus on completed deliveries.

sql: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN order_delivered_customer_date <= order_estimated_delivery_date THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS on_time_delivery_rate FROM orders WHERE order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: This measures the share of orders that were actually delivered to the customer on or before the estimated delivery date. Only orders with a recorded delivery timestamp are included; undelivered orders are excluded from this calculation.

sql: SELECT AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', orders.order_purchase_timestamp, orders.order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_delivery_days FROM orders WHERE orders.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
explanation: This measures the average time from when a customer purchased an order until it was delivered to them. We exclude orders that haven't been delivered yet, since we cannot calculate delivery time for them.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS deal_count FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete
explanation: This counts the number of signed clients whose 90-day post-signature observation window was complete. The filter for window_complete is required because deals signed late in the data period (through November 2018) may not have had a full 90 days to generate revenue, since the commerce data ends in September 2018.

sql: SELECT funnel_leads.origin AS channel, COUNT(DISTINCT deal_outcomes.mql_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT funnel_leads.mql_id) AS conversion_rate FROM funnel_leads LEFT JOIN deal_outcomes ON funnel_leads.mql_id = deal_outcomes.mql_id GROUP BY funnel_leads.origin ORDER BY conversion_rate DESC
explanation: This query measures the share of marketing-qualified leads from each channel that went on to sign. The conversion_rate metric counts distinct leads that became deals divided by all distinct leads, grouped by acquisition channel (organic search, paid search, social, direct traffic, email, referral, display, and others).

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads WHERE origin = 'not_recorded'
explanation: This counts marketing-qualified leads where the acquisition channel is marked as 'not_recorded', meaning the source was not identified in the data capture process.

sql: SELECT business_segment, COUNT(*) AS client_count, AVG(CASE WHEN ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY business_segment HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 ORDER BY attachment_rate DESC
explanation: This query shows the attachment rate—the share of signed clients who generated any revenue in their first 90 days—for each business segment. Only segments with at least twenty signed clients are included. Results are ordered by attachment rate from highest to lowest. The window_complete filter is mandatory to ensure a fair 90-day observation period for all clients.

The layer does not define a "seller state" dimension. The data includes seller performance and order information, but sellers are not joined to a geographical dimension with their state location. The available state dimension is customer_state, which identifies where end customers are located, not where sellers are based. Sellers in this dataset are identified by seller_id but their location is not recorded.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS cancelled_orders FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'canceled'
explanation: This counts the total number of orders with a status of 'canceled'. The orders table includes all orders regardless of status, so we filter to only those marked as cancelled.

sql: SELECT o.order_status, AVG(r.review_score) AS avg_review_score FROM orders o LEFT JOIN order_reviews r ON o.order_id = r.order_id GROUP BY o.order_status ORDER BY avg_review_score DESC
explanation: This query calculates the mean review score (1 to 5) for each order status. Orders are grouped by their status, and the average review score is computed for reviews left on orders in each status category. Orders without reviews are included in the count but contribute no score to the average.

sql: SELECT lead_type, COUNT(*) AS signed_clients FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY lead_type ORDER BY signed_clients DESC
explanation: This query counts the number of signed clients in the acquisition funnel, grouped by their lead type classification. Lead type represents how leads were categorized by size and channel at the point of qualification.

sql: SELECT MEDIAN(revenue_90d) AS median_90d_revenue FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete AND revenue_90d > 0
explanation: This query calculates the median 90-day revenue for signed clients that generated at least some revenue in their first 90 days. It excludes deals outside the complete observation window and clients that never billed (where revenue_90d is 0).

The layer does not define a "category" column or dimension for products. The product table contains only product name, list price, and product series (GTX, MG, GTK). There is no English category field in the available data.

sql: SELECT strftime(first_contact_date, '%Y-%m') AS month, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY strftime(first_contact_date, '%Y-%m') ORDER BY month
explanation: This counts the total number of marketing-qualified leads in the acquisition pipeline, grouped by the month in which they had their first marketing contact. It shows how lead volume varied month by month across the observation period.

sql: SELECT seller_id, revenue_brl, avg_review_score FROM seller_performance ORDER BY revenue_brl DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This query ranks sellers by their lifetime revenue on the marketplace and returns the top five, along with each seller's average review score from customer reviews. Revenue is measured in Brazilian Real (BRL).

sql: SELECT SUM(i.price) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT i.order_id) AS avg_order_value FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id WHERE o.order_status <> 'canceled'
explanation: This calculates the average order value by dividing total item revenue (excluding cancelled orders) by the count of distinct orders. Each order is counted once regardless of how many line items it contains.

sql: SELECT landing_page_id, COUNT(*) AS lead_count FROM funnel_leads GROUP BY landing_page_id ORDER BY lead_count DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This query counts the number of marketing-qualified leads that came through each landing page and shows the top five pages by volume. Each lead is counted once, regardless of which channel or origin drove it to that page.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS signed_clients_no_revenue FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete AND revenue_90d = 0
explanation: This counts signed clients whose first 90 days after signing produced zero revenue. The filter on window_complete ensures we only look at clients who had a full 90-day observation window; deals signed late in the data cannot show revenue by construction. Revenue of 0 is a real outcome meaning the client never billed, not a missing value.

sql: SELECT business_type, MEDIAN(days_to_close) AS median_days_to_close FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY business_type ORDER BY median_days_to_close
explanation: This query shows the median days from first marketing contact to deal signature for each business type of signed clients. I use the median rather than mean because time-to-close distributions are typically skewed, and the median better represents a typical close time.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count FROM orders o JOIN order_reviews r ON o.order_id = r.order_id WHERE r.review_score = 1
explanation: This counts the distinct orders that received at least one review with a score of 1 (the lowest rating). Orders are counted distinctly because one order can have multiple review records attached to it.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT seller_id) AS distinct_sellers FROM order_items
explanation: This counts the number of unique seller IDs that have at least one item line in the order_items table. Each seller appears once in the count regardless of how many items they listed.

sql: SELECT business_segment, SUM(revenue_90d) AS total_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY business_segment ORDER BY total_revenue_90d DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This query sums the revenue billed by signed clients in their first 90 days after closing, grouped by business segment. It includes only deals with a complete 90-day observation window, which is mandatory to avoid undercounting revenue from deals signed late in the data period.

sql: SELECT lead_type, AVG(revenue_90d) AS avg_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete GROUP BY lead_type ORDER BY avg_revenue_90d DESC
explanation: This query measures the average revenue billed by signed clients in their first 90 days, grouped by lead type (a size and channel classification assigned at qualification). The filter on window_complete ensures we only look at deals that had a full 90-day observation window to generate revenue—without this filter, deals signed late would show artificially low revenue simply because the data collection ended before they had 90 days to bill.

sql: SELECT won_month, COUNT(*) AS clients_signed FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY won_month ORDER BY won_month
explanation: This counts the number of signed clients (deals) grouped by the month they were signed. Each row in deal_outcomes represents one signed client, so a simple count by month shows how many clients signed in each period.

sql: SELECT AVG(freight_value) AS avg_freight_per_item FROM order_items
explanation: This query calculates the average freight cost across all item lines in the marketplace orders. Each row in order_items represents one item line within an order, so the average is computed directly over those lines.

sql: SELECT AVG(item_count) AS avg_items_per_order FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS item_count FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id)
explanation: This query counts the number of item lines within each order, then averages those counts. It tells you the typical number of product lines in an order.

sql: SELECT seller_performance.seller_id, seller_performance.reviews FROM seller_performance ORDER BY seller_performance.reviews DESC LIMIT 5
explanation: This query retrieves the five sellers with the highest review counts from the seller performance table, which tracks lifetime reviews per seller on the marketplace.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN origin = 'paid_search' THEN mql_id END) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT mql_id) AS paid_search_proportion FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This measures the share of signed clients whose original marketing contact came through paid search. It counts the distinct number of deals from the paid_search channel divided by the total number of deals.

sql: SELECT c.customer_state, AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', o.order_purchase_timestamp, o.order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_delivery_days FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL AND o.order_status <> 'canceled' GROUP BY c.customer_state HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) >= 500 AND AVG(DATE_DIFF('day', o.order_purchase_timestamp, o.order_delivered_customer_date)) > 20 ORDER BY avg_delivery_days DESC
explanation: This query finds Brazilian states where delivered orders took an average of more than 20 days from purchase to delivery, among states with at least 500 delivered orders. It excludes cancelled orders and undelivered orders where the delivery timestamp is missing.

sql: SELECT order_status, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY order_status ORDER BY order_count DESC
explanation: This query counts the distinct number of orders for each order status category. Since each order can have multiple item lines, we count distinct order IDs to avoid inflating the count.

sql: SELECT deal_outcomes.origin AS channel, AVG(CASE WHEN deal_outcomes.ever_sold THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS attachment_rate FROM deal_outcomes WHERE deal_outcomes.window_complete GROUP BY deal_outcomes.origin ORDER BY attachment_rate DESC
explanation: This query shows the share of signed clients that generated any revenue in their first 90 days, broken down by the marketing channel that produced the lead. The window_complete filter ensures we only count deals with a full 90-day observation window, as required for this metric.

sql: SELECT SUM(revenue_90d) AS total_revenue_90d FROM deal_outcomes WHERE window_complete
explanation: This query sums the revenue billed by all signed clients in their first 90 days after signing. The filter on window_complete is required: it excludes deals signed too late in the observation period to have a full 90-day window, which would otherwise artificially deflate the total.

sql: SELECT behaviour_primary, COUNT(*) AS client_count FROM deal_outcomes GROUP BY behaviour_primary ORDER BY client_count DESC
explanation: This query counts the number of signed clients by their primary behaviour profile. Behaviour profiles classify how clients conduct business on the marketplace, and this shows which profile appears most frequently among the 842 clients in the acquisition data.

sql: SELECT MAX(days_to_close) AS longest_days_to_close FROM deal_outcomes
explanation: This query finds the maximum days_to_close value across all signed clients (deals), showing the longest time from first marketing contact to contract signature in the dataset.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS seller_count FROM seller_performance WHERE avg_review_score < 3
explanation: This counts the number of sellers in the marketplace whose lifetime average review score (on a 1-5 scale) falls below 3. The data excludes cancelled orders.
